https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

The BitChat episode raises a much bigger question than one app.

BitChat is designed to allow nearby phones to communicate through Bluetooth mesh, without depending on mobile internet, SIM cards or a central messaging server. Its popularity reportedly surged in India during protests where internet connectivity was restricted.

On 3 October 2026, Apple removed BitChat from the Indian App Store following a government direction under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act. The Internet Freedom Foundation has questioned the legality and proportionality of blocking an entire communications application, particularly when the specific allegedly unlawful content has not been publicly identified.

The democratic principle is simple:

Internet shutdown ≠ shutdown of citizenship.

A democracy must be able to distinguish between:
• unlawful conduct and lawful communication;
• specific harmful content and an entire communications tool;
• legitimate security concerns and disproportionate restrictions;
• regulation and suppression of the ability of citizens to communicate.

The answer to concerns about misuse should be due process, transparency and targeted action—not automatically making ordinary citizens unable to communicate with one another.

The government should publicly disclose the legal basis and specific grounds for the blocking order, and affected developers should have meaningful access to legal remedies.

Technology will keep evolving. Democratic safeguards must evolve with it.

Protect communication. Protect due process. Protect the constitutional space for peaceful citizenship.

Under Article 19 of the Indian Constitution, citizens do not have an absolute right to protest; authorities can legally restrict or stop a protest under specific, defined conditions.

Constitutional Basis

• Article 19(1)(a): Guarantees freedom of speech and expression.

• Article 19(1)(b): Guarantees the right to assemble peacefully and without arms.

• Article 19(2) & 19(3): Allow the State to place "reasonable restrictions" on these rights.

👉🏼 Grounds to Restrict or Stop a Protest

Authorities can curtail, disperse, or deny permission for a protest based on:

• Public Order: Preventing riots, violence, or severe public disruption.

• Sovereignty and Integrity of India: Protecting national security and unity.

• Security of the State: Safeguarding government installations or preventing incitement to offences.

• Public Convenience: The Supreme Court (such as in the Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police / Shaheen Bagh case) has ruled that public ways and spaces cannot be occupied indefinitely or in a way that blocks essential traffic and inconveniences the public.

Legal Mechanisms Used by Police

• Prior Permission & Designated Spaces: Police can require advance notice or mandate that demonstrations occur only in specific designated areas (like Jantar Mantar in Delhi) rather than arbitrarily blocking vital public corridors.

• Prohibitory Orders (Section 163 of BNSS / formerly Section 144 of CrPC): Magistrates can issue orders banning the assembly of five or more people in an area if there is an apprehension of danger or disturbance.

• Dispersal and Preventive Arrests: Under provisions like Section 148 and Section 170 of the BNSS, authorities are legally empowered to disperse unlawful or violent assemblies and make preventive arrests if peaceful bounds are crossed.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

Our South African journalists are up to standard. Activists and public figures must not think journalists are cowards or idiots.

The procuments related to Jacinta Zuma including g tenders won over time is generally announced to the public as part of normal tender reporting. 

Is there evidence that these state procurements were published especially the 3 year agricultural support contract.

 This procurement information was readily accessible to the public as part of normal state routines. 

Why then did Jacinta Zuma not simply confirm this public information to the journalist.

 Did Jacinta ever mislead the public about her participation in state tenders

Yes, evidence indicates that these state procurements were published. 

Media investigations into March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma and her husband, Xolani Zuma, relied directly on publicly available records. This includes National Treasury procurement data, provincial state tender portals, and government expenditure reports. 

Specifically, the 36-month "farmer support and development" contract awarded to their company, XJ Family Enterprise, by the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, was documented in the provincial government's capital expenditure projections for the 2026/27 financial year. 

Why Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma Did Not Initially Confirm the Information

Rather than verifying the records when approached by a News24 journalist on 7 October 2026, Ngobese-Zuma declined to answer detailed questions, dismissed the inquiry, and threatened legal action. 

Her immediate public strategy involved posting the journalist's written inquiry and phone number directly on Facebook, accusing the publication of spreading lies to distract the public. 

While she did not explicitly clarify her private motives for avoiding a standard confirmation at that exact moment, public analysis and her subsequent actions suggest several factors:

Political Contradiction: As a populist activist campaigning heavily against undocumented immigration and criticizing state operations, being exposed as a beneficiary of multimillion-rand state contracts worth nearly R12 million created a significant narrative conflict. 

Deflection Strategy: Sharing the journalist's private information shifted public attention away from the data and onto the media itself, mobilizing her loyal social media base to defend her. 

Shifting Her Stance: Once the story was fully published, her public rhetoric changed. 

She later defended her participation on social media, arguing that since foreign nationals benefit from lawful procurement frameworks, there is nothing inherently wrong with South African citizens bidding for and executing the same legal contracts. 

Did She Mislead the Public?
Whether she intentionally "misled" the public depends on how her initial reactions are characterized. 

While she did not explicitly deny owning businesses, her immediate response was to label the journalist's inquiry as "lies" and challenge the media to prove the allocations. 

Because the underlying procurement data is entirely factual and sourced directly from government books, publicly calling the investigative inquiries "lies" has been widely critiqued by journalists and observers as an attempt to obscure the truth and dodge public scrutiny.

 Her husband, Xolani Zuma, took a different approach, refraining from aggressive denials and offering to explain the nature of his legal and agricultural state contracts in an interview after publication.

Violence and intense operational disruptions have severely compromised safety at South African Refugee Reception Offices (RROs).

 In response to this acute crisis, the Department of Home Affairs (DHA) officially withdrew its internal directive regarding the immediate intake of asylum seeker applications on Friday, 9 October 2026. 

The immediate trigger for the crisis was a 28 September directive instructing RROs to process all asylum seekers—including those who entered unlawfully—in order to comply with a July Constitutional Court ruling. 

Within days, the sudden influx of applicants overwhelmed facilities and catalyzed coordinated public unrest, which officials directly attribute to a mix of criminal actions and strategic political instigation. [1] 

The Criminal Dimension: Localized Violence and Looting

The demonstrations rapidly escalated into targeted criminality across key metros, particularly in Durban
  and Soweto.

• Property Destruction: Riots led to the torching of at least 24 vehicles (14 in Durban and 10 in Soweto). Protesters in Durban also set fire to a commercial scrapyard linked to a foreign national. [1]

• Intimidation and Assault: Clashes broke out directly outside the Che Guevara Road RRO in Durban, where anti-immigrant groups carrying weapons (such as sticks and sjamboks) physically blocked and intimidated both asylum seekers and DHA staff. Multiple people were hospitalised, and a police officer was assaulted during the unrest. [1]

• Law Enforcement Response: The Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) on Migration reported that at least 30 individuals—including identified ringleaders—were arrested for public violence, illegal gathering, and obstruction. [1]

The Political Dimension: Disinformation and Election Exploitation

The instability has been heavily fueled by political stakeholders utilizing the migration debate as leverage ahead of the upcoming 2026 Municipal Elections on 4 November 2026. [1]

• The Disinformation Campaign: Home Affairs Minister Leon Schreiber noted that a widespread, deliberate social media campaign weaponized the Constitutional Court's order. 

False claims were circulated alleging that the judgment granted automatic citizenship, voting rights, or blanket amnesty to undocumented migrants. 

The DHA has partnered with the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) to track down the network of bot accounts responsible for inciting the panic. [1]

• Organised Anti-Migrant Groups: Prominent political and civic pressure groups, such as Operation Dudula and March and March (led by Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma), explicitly coordinated the shutdowns.

 These groups capitalized on local anxieties surrounding high unemployment and public service strain, demands that the ruling be reviewed, and calls for immediate mass deportations. [1]
 
Next Steps for Operations

Having officially revoked the immediate processing directive to protect public safety, the government is currently operating in a temporary administrative holding pattern. IMC Chair and Minister of Justice Mmamoloko Kubayi
 announced that the state is considering approaching the courts for a supervisory order.

 This would give the Department of Home Affairs a legally sanctioned suspension period to safely build the administrative, infrastructural, and security capacity needed to comply with the constitutional ruling without triggering further national unrest. [1]

जिस मस्क को कभी भारत में जेल जाने से डर लगता था, उस मस्क को क्या हुआ है? क्यों पिनक गए हैं, चिंता की बात होनी चाहिए। सूचना प्रसारण मंत्रालय के मंत्री को एक्स के किसी मैनेजर को बुलाकर पूछना चाहिए कि तुम्हारे मालिक नरेंद्र मोदी को छोड़ अंबानी को कैसे प्रधानमंत्री लिख रहे हैं? यह शपथ कब हुआ है? फोटो दिखाओ? मस्क, अंबानी, अदाणी, सरकार इन सबके बीच जो हो रहा है, उनके बीच सही बात क्या है, किसी को पता तो है नहीं। कौन किसे मैनेज कर रहा है, पर्दे के पीछे के पर्दे के पीछे कौन-कौन है, यह जान लेने से क्या बदल जाता है। मगर प्रधानमंंत्री अंबानी हैं, ये कब बदल गया? राहुल गांधी तो वोट चोरी को प्रधानमंत्री, गृहमंत्री और ज्ञानेश कुमार के प्रोजेक्ट तक ही देख पा रहे हैं, इसके ऊपर का भी मामला है क्या? 

वैसे इस प्लेटफार्म के लिए मस्क आपका शुक्रिया। ठीक है सरकार के कहने पर आप भी पोस्ट हटा देते हैं लेकिन आदमी अपनी बात तो लिख पा रहा है। अगर एक्स करोल बाग के किसी टाइकून का प्लेटफार्म होता तो हम लोगों के प्लेटफार्म के आगे बैरिकेड लगवा देता और डिलीट कर देता। इसलिए आपके पोस्ट पर इधर के उद्योगपति लोग भी चुप हैं। आसान नहीं है आपकी तरह लब-लब कुछ भी बोल देना। इधर सारा आंत्रोपन्योरशिप सरकार से लाइसेंस, ठेका, ज़मीन वाले प्रोजेक्ट लेने में लगा रहता है। ज़िलाधिकारी से लेकर सचिव के चक्कर काटने में लगा रहता है। एक प्रोडक्ट ढंग का नहीं बनता। अपने प्रोडेक्ट को ग्लोबल लेवल पर पहुंचाने के बजाए 24 घंटा इसी में लगे रहते हैं कि सरकार से क्या मिल सकता है। आपको भी वही झेलना पड़ेगा। आप भारत आओ, दीवाली का टाइम है, गिफ्ट-विफ्ट लेकर आओ, बात समझो, आप देखना यही मंत्री लोग आपके साथ कैसे फोटो खिंचाते हैं। आओ तो सही, पूरी सरकार बिछी मिलेगी। मुस्कुरा दोगे पीएम साहब को देख कर तो गोदी मीडिया हेडलाइन बना देगा। अपनी वैल्यू समझो आप। कॉकरोच दिल्ली आ गए हैं और आप उधर से ही पोस्ट फायर किए जा रहे हो। COME.

इसीलिए मस्क जी, भारत के प्रधानमंत्री का नाम नरेंद्र मोदी है। अंबानी नहीं है। भारत में आपकी जीवनी हिन्दी में भी छप चुकी है। आपकी माँ मेय मस्क जी की किताब जब औरत सोचती है, राजकमल प्रकाशन से छप चुकी है।आप एक मामूली पॉलिसी निर्णय को लेकर पिनके हुए हैं, यहां तो करोड़ों लोगों के वोट काट दिए गए हैं। वोट का अधिकार छीन लिया गया है। बात को समझो आप। सोशल मीडिया की तरह वोटर को ब्लॉक कर दिया जाता है। नेता प्रतिपक्ष को धक्का दिया जाता है। स्टार लिंक लेकर आ भी गए होते तो क्या हो जाता, आपका भी आज सीपी और चार किलोमीटर के दायरे में बंद रहता। अच्छा हुआ है आप नहीं आए। वैसे अगर स्टार लिंक का कोई पर्सनल लिंक है तो व्हाट्स एप पर भेज देना। आज जंतर-मंतर से वीडियो अपलिंक करना है। बच्चों को प्यार देना। प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी की तरफ से भी। हम लोग डर जाते हैं मगर प्यार ज़रूर करते हैं। ख़ुश रहिए।

Meta-owned messaging giant WhatsApp has banned more than 79 lakh accounts in India in the month of March, in compliance with the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

According to the company's monthly compliance report, Between the March 1-31 period, 7,954,000 WhatsApp accounts were banned, and 1,430,000 of these accounts were proactively banned before any reports from users.

Notably, The company received a record 12,782 complaint reports in March in the country, and the records "actioned" were 11.

Between February 1-29, the company had banned "7,628,000 accounts".

text:
BREAKING: FG Shuts Down Over 13 million Social Media Accounts for Offensive Content…takes down 58.9million obscene contents

The federal government has closed down about 13,597,057 social media accounts for offensive content and violations of the code of practice by users of social media platforms such as TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, and X, formerly known as Twitter.

The government action was contained in a Code of Practice 2024 Compliance Report submitted to the government by promoters of interactive computer service platforms such as Google, Microsoft and TikTok, among others.

The Code of Practice was issued jointly by the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), and the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC).

In a statement signed on Wednesday by the Director of Corporate Communications and Media Relations of NITDA, Hajiya Hadiza Umar, the government said a total of 58,909,112 offensive contents were taken down from various platforms.

The statement, which commended Google, Microsoft, and TikTok for their continued compliance with the Code of Practice for Interactive Computer Service Platforms/Internet Intermediaries, also noted that 754,629 were “registered complaints.”
She added that 420,439 contents were removed and re-uploaded following appeals by users.
“The compliance reports provide valuable insights into the platforms’ efforts to address user safety concerns in line with the Code of Practice and the platforms’ community guidelines,” the statement noted.

The statement said, “The submission of these reports marks a significant step towards fostering a safer and responsible digital environment for Nigerian users. TribuneNG reports

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.

Hey everyone, have you been keeping up with this massive development in the Sambhal Masjid survey case? The Supreme Court has just made a ruling that's setting the stage for some real legal fireworks. Let's break this down because it's not just legal mumbo jumbo; it's a significant moment for cultural heritage, religious rights, and historical truth.

What Just Happened?

The Supreme Court, through a bench led by CJI Sanjiv Khanna and Justice Sanjay Kumar, has allowed the Advocate Commissioner to submit the survey report on the Sambhal Mosque to the trial court, but in a sealed cover. This is a big deal because:

1. No Stay Order: The SC didn't put a stay on the trial court's order to survey the mosque. This means the process isn't halted; it's just moving forward under wraps.

2. Masjid Committee's Next Move: The court has directed the Masjid Committee to approach the High Court, indicating that the legal battle is far from over. This gives the committee a chance to contest the survey's implications at a higher judicial level.

3. Sealed Cover Submission: The report will be given in a sealed cover. This is often done in sensitive cases to ensure that the court is the first to review potentially contentious information, maintaining judicial integrity.

Why This Matters:

- Places of Worship Act, 1991: This act was meant to preserve the religious character of places as they existed on August 15, 1947. However, it doesn't apply to monuments protected by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), like the Jama Masjid in Sambhal. This exception is crucial because it opens the door for legal scrutiny that wouldn't be possible under the Act's general protection.

- The Purpose of the Survey: The original case, filed by Advocate Vishnu Shankar Jain, aimed to determine the mosque's character. Now, with the survey report being submitted, it's about getting closer to answering this question. 

- Legal Implications: The Hindu side isn't viewing this as a victory for the Masjid side because the report's submission means the investigation into the mosque's origins and character will continue. The sealed cover ensures that the findings are preserved for judicial review before any public or media speculation.

What's Next?

- Trial Court's Role:*The trial court has a scheduled hearing on January 8. There's no rush to proceed until the Masjid Committee makes its move in the High Court, which could potentially challenge or affirm the survey.

- High Court's Potential Decision: Depending on how the Masjid Committee argues their case, the High Court could either validate the survey's continuation or find grounds to halt or alter the process.

The Broader Conversation:

This isn't just about a piece of land or a structure; it's about history, identity, and legal rights:

- Cultural Heritage: Every stone, every inscription, every architectural feature of a site like this could tell a story of a civilization. If there's evidence suggesting a different historical use of the site, that's a story that needs to be told, preserved, and understood.

- Religious Rights: The sanctity of places of worship is a sensitive topic. For communities, these are not just buildings but embodiments of faith. How do you balance the right to worship with the right to investigate historical claims?

- Legal Precedents: This case could set a precedent for how religious disputes over historical sites are handled in India, especially where ASI protection plays a role. It's a test of how the legal system can navigate through claims of history, archaeology, and religious sentiment.

- Political Undercurrents: Let's not ignore that such cases often have political dimensions. They can influence community relations, electoral politics, and even national security concerns.

Reflections:

- Transparency and Justice: The sealed cover ensures that the findings aren't tampered with or sensationalized before judicial review, promoting a form of transparency where justice is seen to be done by the court first.

- Community Dialogue: This is an opportunity for dialogue between communities. If handled with sensitivity, it could lead to a mutual understanding of history and coexistence.

- Educational Value: Whatever the outcome, this case is a lesson in how history, law, and religion can intersect in modern contexts, offering insights into how societies deal with their past.

While the Supreme Court's decision might seem procedural, it's a pivotal moment in a case that touches on deep historical, cultural, and religious issues. It's a moment for all of us to watch, learn from, and reflect upon. Let's hope that justice, in its truest form, prevails, ensuring that historical truths are respected alongside the rights and sentiments of all involved communities. Keep an eye on this space; it's more than just legal news; it's a narrative of our shared heritage.

*Polycab India was placed under the IBC framework because the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Ahmedabad Bench, admitted an insolvency petition against the company on October 7, 2026, initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).*
Details Behind the Admission
 The Petitioner: The insolvency plea was filed under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) by an operational creditor, Asier Metals Private Limited.
 Claim Amount: The dispute involves an alleged unpaid operational debt of approximately ₹2.79 crore.
 Automatic Exchange Mechanism: Under SEBI and stock exchange surveillance guidelines, the moment an NCLT bench officially admits an insolvency plea against a listed entity, the exchange is required to automatically shift the scrip into the IBC Surveillance Framework. This triggers mandatory risk controls, including removal from the F&O segment, 100% margin requirements, and eventual price-band curbs.
The Company’s Stand
 Commercial Dispute: Polycab has stated that the ₹2.79 crore claim is a pre-existing commercial dispute involving credit notes, ledger reconciliation, and demurrage adjustments rather than financial distress.
 Financial Position: The disputed amount is immaterial relative to Polycab's balance sheet (the company holds over ₹4,000 crore in cash/liquid balances and a net worth exceeding ₹11,000 crore).
 Legal Recourse: Polycab immediately filed an appeal before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) seeking a stay/quashing of the NCLT order.
If the NCLAT grants an interim stay or dismisses the CIRP admission order, Polycab can approach the stock exchanges to review and potentially revoke the IBC surveillance measures.

*Polycab could be at risk of MSCI deletion*: MSCI's India Ineligible Alert Board (IAB) policy explicitly includes India's Enhanced Surveillance Measure (ESM) and Insolvency Resolution Process frameworks on the Bombay Stock Exchange and National Stock Exchange.

Under that policy:
Securities included on the IAB are excluded from the MSCI Equity Universe.
Existing MSCI constituents entering the IAB are deleted on the last business day of the month, with at least two full business days' notice.
Such securities cannot be added back to MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes for 12 months following deletion.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

The Union government’s draft Seeds Bill 2025, now open for public comments until 11 December, arrives not a day too soon. From counterfeit packets in village markets to procurement disputes at mandis, the chain between breeder and farmer has too many weak links.

For Punjab, where seed quality, FCI norms, and groundwater stress intersect, if not collide, every season, this Bill is more than a compliance document. It is a chance to rebuild trust in the most basic input of agriculture.

How is it better than the old law?

Three design shifts from the Seeds Act of 1966 deserve unambiguous support.

First, universal registration of varieties. The 1966 Act essentially regulated only ‘notified’ kinds, leaving a grey market of truthfully labelled seeds outside meaningful oversight. The draft moves toward mandatory registration for all new varieties and a pathway for deemed registration of existing ones. If implemented with predictable timelines and transparent criteria, this closes the back door through which poor-quality seed has circulated for decades.

Second, traceability and digital oversight. The draft emphasises traceability— already feasible through platforms that assign a scannable identity to each lot from breeder to dealer. That lets a farmer verify authenticity at the counter and allows regulators to trace a bad lot swiftly up the chain. Traceability should not be a slogan; it must become a farmer’s everyday tool. Make it mandatory at scale, standardise the QR/barcode, and integrate it with e-invoices so that one scan reveals who produced, processed, stored, and sold the seed, and when.

Third, smarter penalties with measured decriminalisation. Minor technical lapses should not land honest actors in criminal court; serious fraud should. The draft’s graded penalties, with steep fines and custodial terms for spurious and unregistered seed, are a clear improvement over the token fines of the 1966 law. The promise is a system that is both business-friendly and farmer‑protective—if enforcement stays sharp.

Two related moves are consequential for Punjab. One is the shift from a state-by-state dealer licensing culture to centralised accreditation/recognition. That may cut duplication for multi-state firms, but it also risks hollowing out the “last mile” unless states retain day-to-day inspection teeth. The other is price oversight “in emergent situations”. That clause matters in the sowing window, when speculation can shut smallholders out of quality seed.

Federal design at the last mile

The August ruling of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which held that states cannot ban centrally notified hybrid paddy, was a reminder that seed regulation sits across the Centre-state seam. Punjab has since hardened deterrence at its end, making the sale of spurious seeds a non-bailable, cognisable offence, reflecting accumulated anger in the countryside at fly-by-night operators. Industry protests aside, the message from Chandigarh is clear: the deterrent must be felt in the marketplace.

The draft national law should recognise this reality instead of flattening it. Keep national registration and central accreditation if you must—but codify concurrent enforcement powers for states: surprise sampling, seizure, prosecution, and the ability to prescribe local storage and display conditions. Delhi can set standards; inspectors in Moga and Muktsar will enforce them.

Farmers’ vantage point: performance and procurement

From a farmer’s field, regulation is judged by three blunt questions: Did the seed perform? If not, who pays? And will the crop be procured on fair terms?

The draft is strong at the pre-market gate (registration and traceability) and on deterrence. It is notably weaker on compensation when registered seed underperforms despite adoption of the recommended package of practices. Punjab’s last two seasons underlined why this gap matters: disruptive weather, discolouration and moisture contests at mandis, and a milling reluctance toward some hybrids have turned quality disputes into income shocks.

The fix is straightforward. Create a time-bound, no-fault compensation window for clear seed failures, financed by a blend of mandatory manufacturer insurance, a small cess on registrations, and state top-ups in disaster years. Publish the yield-loss formula up front; do not force a small farmer to litigate against a corporate legal team. At the same time, institutionalise pre-season coordination among the Agriculture Ministry, FCI/DFPD, and states on uniform procurement specifications, with a hybrid-specific annexure and pre-declared relaxations for flood years. Let seed standards and procurement norms talk to each other before the first bag is sold.

Let FPOs co-brand seed

Earlier seed‑bill drafts recognised a farmer’s right to save, use, exchange and sell farm‑saved seed, with one caveat: it cannot be sold under a brand name.

The intent was to block quasi‑commercial masquerading without quality assurance. But the rise of Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) changes the calculus. The Union government wants FPOs to aggregate, process, and market produce; it funds them and extends credit and tax support for precisely that reason. If the final Seeds Act mechanically extends a “no brand” caveat to FPO‑aggregated seed, it would hobble a flagship reform.

The harmonising path is clear: permit FPO co-branding of farm-saved seed provided three conditions are met. First, lots must pass notified minimum standards in an accredited lab. Second, full traceability, including grower IDs and storage logs that must be uploaded to the national portal. Third, liability must sit with the FPO’s board for false claims, not with individual members. That keeps out fly-by-night branding while letting farmer institutions move up the value chain.

Dealer liability, without scapegoating the honest

Punjab has thousands of small input dealers who act as the farmer’s first line of advice and supply. They cannot become the system’s whipping boy for failures they did not cause.

The law should adopt a manufacturer-first liability rule on germination and genetic purity for factory-sealed packs, while giving dealers a safe harbour if they sell sealed lots, meet prescribed storage conditions, keep traceable invoices, and hand over required samples during inspections. Penal exposure should bite dealers who tamper, knowingly misbrand, or operate outside the accredited chain. That keeps deterrence where it belongs—on those who cheat—without driving legitimate retailers out of business.

Traceability as a price stabiliser, not just a cop’s tool

If the Centre retains emergency price-control powers, anchor them in transparent triggers captured by the traceability system: inventory-to-sowing-window ratios, abnormal interstate price spreads, and unusual movement patterns. Public dashboards would discipline prices before official fiat is needed, and they would help states intervene in time. Let the QR on a packet be both a shield against fraud and a signal for markets.

Water‑wise seed choices backed by procurement

For Punjab, seed policy is also water policy. Short-duration, water-efficient paddy, as well as non-paddy kharif options, must get fast-track registration and agronomy support.

But farmers will not switch varieties or crops unless procurement policy aligns. That means assured purchase pathways for water-saving options, predictable miller acceptance for hybrids, and extension support that links seed choice to groundwater outcomes. Otherwise, the rational farmer will cling to long-duration staples that mills prefer and FCI buys on familiar specs.

It is essential to stitch seed regulation to FCI procurement policy for hybrid paddy so that what farmers sow confidently in June is not rejected quibblingly in October.

Minor tweaks before enactment: a Punjab‑first checklist

Keep central registration, but write state enforcement powers into the statute.

Clarify the liability chain: manufacturer first; dealer safe harbour for sealed, properly stored, traceable stock; strict penalties for tampering and misbranding.

Make compensation real with a time‑bound, no‑fault window and a published formula.

Hard‑wire coordination with FCI on uniform specs and a hybrid‑specific annexure, with pre‑declared relaxations in disaster years.

Use traceability to improve competition and price discovery, not merely to police.

Greenlight FPO co‑branding under standards‑plus‑traceability, with board‑level liability.

Invest in accredited seed labs and risk‑based inspections so enforcement is fast, fair and science‑led.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.
