Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

The BBC has announced a two-part documentary about J.K. Rowling. And already, its choice of language raises questions.

The BBC’s press release says the series will explore Rowling’s “dramatic rise, cultural influence and contested legacy”, describing how the Harry Potter author became “one of Britain’s most polarising public figures”.

According to the programme makers, her “unflinching personal beliefs have sparked a fraught and divisive dialogue that continues to this day”.

But whose framing is this?

Rowling has become one of the UK’s most prominent defenders of women’s sex-based rights, using her considerable influence and wealth to challenge policies she believes undermine those rights.

Yet the BBC’s announcement appears to frame her beliefs as the source of division, rather than asking why defending those rights has become so contentious.

Women’s rights do get a brief mention - but only in the context of how her supporters see her, contrasted with critics who describe her as an opponent of “trans equality”.

Words matter in journalism. So do the editorial assumptions behind them.

Of course, we haven’t seen the documentary yet. So we’ll reserve judgment until the show is aired. 

But when a broadcaster describes a woman’s defence of sex-based rights in terms of her “contested legacy” and “divisive” beliefs, it’s reasonable to ask what assumptions are already shaping the story.

We’ll be watching with interest.

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

The audit that marks every place a reader could stop reading your page.

It judges the joins between sentences, never the sentences themselves. Paste it into a fresh chat with your copy underneath and nothing else.

A reader decides at every full stop whether to read the next sentence. Read the draft the way a busy stranger on a phone would and report where that decision goes against the writer. Judge the joins between sentences, never the craft of a sentence. A well-made sentence can be an exit, and a plain one can pull.

Read as a stranger
Judge only the copy. Ignore any brief, offer, fact sheet or earlier conversation, because a reader who knows the product answers the page's questions from memory and marks gaps closed that a real reader could not close. If you can hand this job to a subagent or a fresh session that receives only the copy and these instructions, do that.

Step 1: Split and number
Split the copy into units and number them. One unit per sentence. A headline, subhead, bullet or one-line paragraph counts as one unit even without a full stop. Print the numbered list first so the split can be checked.

Step 2: Ask two questions at every unit
1. Does this unit give the reader something? It gives something when it answers what an earlier unit opened, or adds a fact, picture, claim or turn the reader did not already have.
2. If the reader stopped right after this unit, would they feel they had left something unfinished? If yes, name what is still open, specifically, in a few words.

Step 3: Classify each unit
- LINK: gives something and leaves something open. This is the slide working.
- EXIT: gives something and leaves nothing open. The reader can stop here feeling finished.
- SIGNPOST: leaves something open but gives nothing of its own. "Here's why." "But there's more." "That brings us to the product." A question that the next unit answers without the question itself adding anything is a signpost. Delete it and the reader loses only the nudge.
- DEAD: gives nothing and leaves nothing open.

Judge every unit as if the reader might stop there, including the last. If the copy is an excerpt, the last unit should still hand the reader into what follows.

Step 4: Track what is owed
List every question or promise the copy opens. Mark each one paid when a later unit answers it. Anything unpaid at the end is OWED, with the unit that opened it. In an excerpt that is expected, and the writer has to confirm the rest of the page pays it. A promise the page never keeps does more damage than an exit.

Output
One line per unit, in order:
7. EXIT
8. LINK — open: what actually works, then?
13. SIGNPOST — answered by 14, adds nothing of its own

Then a summary:
- Counts: LINK, EXIT, SIGNPOST and DEAD, and EXIT plus DEAD as a share of all units.
- Runs: every stretch of two or more EXIT or DEAD units in a row, by unit number. These get fixed first, because two finished sentences in a row give the reader permission to leave.
- Owed: each unpaid question or promise and the unit that opened it.
- Fix first: the three exits that cost the most, with one line on why. Weigh exits near the top of the piece and just before the offer most heavily.

Rules
- Do not rewrite, suggest wording or recommend cuts. Report and stop. The repair belongs to the writer.
- Every open item must name something specific. "The reader wants to know more" names nothing, so a unit with no better reason is an EXIT.
- Mark any call you are unsure of with (?) rather than forcing it.

Report: White House Fears UK Apple iCloud Backdoor Targets Trump, Farage | Ken Macon, Reclaim The Net

The New Statesman is reporting that a White House security official expects the UK to use the backdoor it wants to build into Apple's iCloud – through a secret court order – to spy on the Trump administration and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

The magazine said it had seen a message sent in September from the official to a colleague, which reads: "The UK is making another attempt to put a backdoor on iCloud. This time by their secret court. They're going to lean on a court order to justify it. They will use this back door to spy on the administration and Nigel Farage."

The report does not show that anyone has actually been spied on in this way, and it's obviously alarmist, but the message reveals the fear is present inside the US administration, so at least people are aware of what the UK is doing to undermine privacy.

It is also a perfect example of how a backdoor built to catch criminals is actually a tool that can be used by whoever happens to have it at their disposal, including against political opponents – and allies.

The UK is keeping the order so secret that Apple was able to brief the US Vice President about it - but not the US Congress.

The UK first tried to get Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, through the country's Investigatory Powers Act, and a secret technical capability notice (TCN). The order was later changed to cover only UK users, after the US put pressure on its ally.

Apple never built that backdoor, at least as far as we know. Instead, it withdrew its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users, and new UK users are still unable to turn it on.

Apple has also said that it has "never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products and services and never will."

In June, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan wrote to UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to warn that if reports about the UK order were true, it would mean that the country is building "backdoors into their encrypted services."

Jordan said that would put at risk the security of US citizens' data.

In September, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Republican Representative Warren Davidson wrote to the UK’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal to express their concern over the secret order, saying that the UK was being “wholly inappropriate” in preventing Apple from discussing the issue with US Congress.

"The U.K. government's unprecedented demands for secrecy in this matter undermine democratic governance in both the United States and the U.K., and needlessly strain the relationship between our two nations," the two congressmen wrote.

Weakening encryption in consumer software, the letter said, “introduces critical vulnerabilities that can be exploited by hostile foreign actors.”

Apple went to the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), which hears complaints about surveillance, to try to have the UK order revoked. Privacy International and Liberty have a separate challenge before the same court.

The UK government will neither confirm nor deny that the order exists. But Ben Jaffey KC, who represents Privacy International and Liberty, told the tribunal that "the horse has long bolted."

"The fact that Apple even needed to ask permission confirms there is a TCN," Jaffey said.

Meanwhile, Neil Sheldon KC, acting for the government, said the home secretary's position was "neither irrational nor unsupported by evidence."

In February 2025, Reclaim The Net reported that the UK was trying to force Apple to give it access to all iCloud users' encrypted cloud backups around the world, and that Apple had in the meantime pulled its strongest encryption, Advanced Data Protection, from UK users.

In September 2025, we reported that Farage had told the US Congress that the UK's Online Safety Act was a threat not only to free speech, but also to encryption.

In June, we reported about Jordan's letter to Mahmood, warning that the UK order could compromise data of US citizens.

A backdoor does not check who is asking to use it, or why – and the officials worried about it being turned on Farage and the Trump administration are essentially describing why nobody should have a backdoor.

Scripture rules the Church in the same way that truth rules reason.

But to claim Scripture as the sole authority is cyclical reasoning, because it was the Church that defined what constitutes Scripture.

Picture this: a wealthy man dies and leaves behind a will to distribute his assets after his death, and he has assigned an executor of the will to ensure that his intentions are correctly followed. But his family disputes the authority of the executor and claims “the will alone governs the estate.” But they quickly fall into bickering with one another about what each line of the will really means, and some even begin doubting the veracity of the will — because without the chain of custody, how can they know it’s the real thing?

Thus an executor becomes a legal and practical necessity in order to solve these disputes before they even arise. The executor knew the deceased man and his intentions, and can faithfully execute them — and, crucially, no one else has equal authority to him, and in that way conflicts are minimized and family unity is preserved.

In order for the Bible’s truths to be faithfully interpreted and taught, there must be an interpreter with binding authority over the whole Church. Otherwise it descends into endless bickering and conflict with no resolution in sight. And that is, unfortunately, exactly what the Reformation produced.

Election Commission of India 🎯

1. What is it?
The Election Commission of India (ECI) is an independent body. It conducts elections in India. Its main job is to make sure elections are free and fair.

It was set up on 25 January 1950. This day is now National Voters’ Day.

Headquarters: Nirvachan Sadan, New Delhi.

2. Constitutional basis
The ECI gets its power from Article 324 of the Constitution.

Article 324 says the Commission has the superintendence, direction and control of:
- elections to Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha)
- elections to State Legislatures
- elections of the President and the Vice-President

Note: Local elections (panchayats and municipalities) are not done by the ECI. They are done by the State Election Commissions.

3. Composition
The Commission has three members:
- one Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)
- two Election Commissioners (ECs)

The CEC is the chairman. Decisions are taken by majority.

The President can also appoint Regional Commissioners to help during big elections, after talking to the Commission.

(As of 2026: Shri Gyanesh Kumar is the Chief Election Commissioner. Dr Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Dr Vivek Joshi are Election Commissioners.)

4. Appointment
The President appoints the CEC and the Election Commissioners.

Under the 2023 law, a Selection Committee recommends the names. The committee has:
- the Prime Minister
- a Union Cabinet Minister chosen by the Prime Minister
- the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the largest opposition party)

5. Term and removal
- Term: 6 years, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
- They cannot be reappointed to the same post.
- The CEC can be removed only in the same way as a Supreme Court judge (by Parliament, with a special majority).
- Other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the recommendation of the CEC.
- Their salary and conditions cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.

6. Main functions
- Prepare and revise the electoral rolls (voter lists).
- Conduct elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
- Decide the election schedule and polling dates.
- Recognise political parties as national or state parties.
- Allot election symbols to parties and candidates.
- Enforce the Model Code of Conduct during elections.
- Cancel polls if there is booth capturing, violence, or other serious problems.
- Advise the President or Governor on disqualification of members (for example, under the anti-defection law in some cases).
- Register political parties.

7. Important powers
- It can supervise the whole election process.
- It can give directions to election officers.
- It can use government staff for election work (Article 324(6)).
- It can postpone or cancel an election in a constituency if the situation is not fair.
- It monitors election spending and can take action against violations.

8. Why it is independent
- Fixed term and security of tenure.
- Removal of the CEC is difficult (same as a Supreme Court judge).
- Conditions of service cannot be reduced after appointment.
- It does not work under any ministry during elections.

9. Quick facts to remember
- Constitutional body under Article 324.
- Started: 25 January 1950.
- Multi-member body since 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs).
- Does not conduct panchayat or municipal elections.
- Motto idea: free, fair and transparent elections.
- Helpline: 1950.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
The battlefield doesn't check your follower count.

Every few weeks, Indian defence tech gets a new hero. A slick launch video. A funding headline. "Indigenous" in bold, "made in India" in the caption, and somewhere in the footnotes, an open-source stack, a white-labelled import, and a codebase an AI wrote over the weekend.

The applause is loud. The deployment orders are silent.

Let me be fair: open source is a great foundation, importing to learn is smart, and AI-assisted coding is a real superpower. None of these are the problem. The problem is when we confuse a demo with a capability, and visibility with viability.

A drone that flies beautifully in a Bengaluru tech park has passed exactly one test: the Bengaluru tech park. The real exams are harder:
→ Heavy electronic jamming
→ Desert dust, mountain cold, and coastal salt
→ A soldier with gloves on, no Wi-Fi, and zero patience
→ A foreign supplier who stops answering emails mid-conflict

You can't growth-hack your way through those.

Somewhere, there's a team without a PR agency, a podcast tour, or a viral reel. They've failed field trials, rebuilt the hardware twice, and own every line of their firmware. You haven't heard of them. Our forces probably will.

Before you celebrate the next defence "unicorn," ask:
1️⃣ Who has actually used it, and would they use it again?
Not a demo for officials, but a unit that ran it in jamming, dust, and cold, and still asked for more.

2️⃣ Remove every open-source module, imported part, and AI-generated line. What's left that's truly yours?
If the answer fits on one slide, that's not a product. It's packaging.

3️⃣ If a foreign supplier switched you off tonight, how many days could you keep delivering?
And how long would it take to replace them with an Indian source?

4️⃣ Which certifications and qualification standards have you cleared, and which are you "working towards"?
In defence, "working towards" usually means "not yet."

5️⃣ Who audits your code and firmware, and where does your data go?
In defence, "we trust our vendor" is the wrong answer.
If the answers are vague, the capability probably is too.

Reach gets you followers. Reliability gets you contracts.
Hype raises a round. Hardware wins a war.

Let's back the founders who build for the frontline, not the feed.

Ask harder questions. Build real things. Put the budget in R&D, not in reels.

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
Trump Has Golden Opportunity To Blow Up Climate Agenda’s Crown Jewel | Audrey Streb, Daily Caller News Foundation

The Trump administration is on the precipice of ending the Endangerment Finding, a rule that Democrats have used for years to impose harsh climate regulations, energy policy experts told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

The Endangerment Finding, established in 2009 under the Obama Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), rules that greenhouse gasses including carbon dioxide can be regulated for the sake of human health and the environment. The underlying science was contested when the EPA established the rule, and the Endangerment Finding has since been used to impose draconian rules on power plants that have helped lead to closures across the country and teed up Democrat policies that have forced electric vehicles and appliances onto consumers, energy sector experts told the DCNF.

“The Endangerment Finding was the result of a highly politicized process relying on cherry-picked data meant to appease the wants of climate extremists. It quickly became a favorite tool of Democrat administrations and their left-wing allies to manipulate the economy in favor of their politically-preferred technologies like wind, solar and electric vehicles,” Mandy Gunasekara, author and former EPA Chief of Staff under the first Trump administration, told the DCNF. “The effects of the regulatory schemes built off of the Endangerment Finding are far-reaching and costly. The Endangerment Finding has led to higher energy costs, unreliable electricity grids, lost jobs and a shift of investment to overseas countries like China and India that have lackluster environmental standards.”

The EPA announced that the agency is formally reconsidering the Endangerment Finding on March 12 in collaboration with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and other agencies. OMB received a request from EPA on June 30 regarding the 2009 Endangerment Finding, though the contents have not yet been publicized.

“The proposal will be published for public notice and comment once it has completed interagency review and been signed by the Administrator,” an EPA spokesperson told the DCNF.

In April 2007, the Supreme Court ruled in Massachusetts vs. EPA that greenhouse gases are air pollutants that can be regulated under the Clean Air Act, setting the precedent enabling the Endangerment Finding two years later.

Stringent rules on power plants that stem from the Endangerment Finding have led to closures of coal facilities around the U.S. and weakened the electrical grid, spiking the risk of blackouts, experts have explained to the DCNF previously. After years of static electricity demand, the wave of power plant closures and the anticipation of new data centers has led to projections that the U.S. may be unable to meet its power needs in the near future, according to industry experts and a recent Department of Energy (DOE) report.

“We’re now at a point where we’re facing frequent blackouts… because there’s too much wind and solar in the system,” Myron Ebell, former director for the Center for Energy and Environment at the Competitive Enterprise Institute and leader of the Trump EPA transition team in 2016, told the DCNF. Ebell explained that energy technology like coal provides baseload power, and a heavy reliance on intermittent sources like wind and solar tanks the reliability of the electrical grid. He also noted that there is a correlation between high electricity costs and a strong dependence on resources like wind and solar.

The Endangerment Finding has not only led to strict regulations that have ultimately weakened the electric grid, but it has also allowed for policies that police vehicle emissions, Ebell told the DNCF.

“The consequences of the Endangerment Finding are people being forced to buy vehicles they don’t want,” Ebell said, adding that the One Big Beautiful Bill act did a lot to aid consumer choice as it reduced the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standard violation penalty to $0.

“Now automakers can go ahead and start producing the vehicles Americans want to buy,” Ebell said. He also noted that the Clean Air Act was not designed to regulate carbon dioxide, arguing that it does not do so effectively and that Massachusetts vs. EPA is not a solid legal ruling.

“It’s one of the really most incoherent and poorly argued Supreme Court decisions you can find,” Ebell told the DCNF. “The justices on the majority side really wanted to get on the global warming bandwagon, and they just didn’t want to miss out and be on the wrong side of history.”

...

Gunasekara argued that the scientific data chosen to justify the Endangerment Finding did not consider the benefits of carbon dioxide, and that the models predicting worst-case scenarios have been “disproven by what we’ve experienced in real life.” Some key scientific points were drawn from the fourth United Nations Climate Assessment, which is now almost 20 years old, Gunasekara pointed out, noting that the most recent report is the Sixth Assessment Report.

“The Trump Administration should make its decisions based on the latest and greatest science. The Endangerment Finding does not meet this standard and should no longer be used as a basis for ineffective, highly politicized regulations,” Gunasekara said.

Other critics in the energy sector agree that the Endangerment Finding was not decided on the best scientific evidence.

“The problem is they’ve taken the alarmism way out of proportion,” Willie Soon, astrophysicist and geoscientist who conducts research for the Center for Environmental Research and Earth Sciences (CERES,) told the DNCF. He argues that the scientific evidence available in 2007 when Massachusetts vs. EPA was decided was “boldly untenable,” and that the EPA engaged in “deliberate cherry-picking.”

Diana Furchtgott-Roth, director of the Heritage Foundation’s Center for Energy, Climate, and Environment, told the DCNF that though the data supporting the Endangerment Finding might have come from well-intentioned scientists, it is now outdated.

“It’s about time the Endangerment Finding was rolled back formally,” Furchtgott-Roth said, arguing that the EPA “already rolled back the Endangerment Finding de facto” in June’s proposed repeals and reforms of Obama- and Biden-era emissions rules on power plants.

If the EPA proposed a rule to roll back the whole Endangerment Finding, it would make its way through the federal rulemaking process. The proposed rule would be open to public comment for at least 30 days in the Federal Register before Zeldin could sign it, though significant or major rules are often required to have a 60-day implementation delay.

OMB did not respond to the DNCF’s request for comment.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Your bank account got frozen overnight. No notice, no call, no FIR against you. The bank just says “cyber cell instructions.”

This is happening to ordinary people across India every day. Here is what the law actually says, and what you should do. 🧵

Dear @CoinDCX Team,Ceo @smtgpt 

I am writing to raise a very serious concern regarding my recent withdrawal from CoinDCX.

=> Last month, I placed a withdrawal request (under $1000 USDT) from CoinDCX to my SBI Bank account. Despite paying all applicable taxes including 1% TDS and 28% tax (total 29%) my transaction was blocked by the bank. Later, I received both an email and a phone call instructing me to visit the bank in person. Upon visiting, I was informed that a special notice from Cyber Cell India had been issued regarding my transaction, and I was questioned about my trading history.

My questions are very clear:

1. After paying 29% tax on trading gains, why are my funds still being flagged as gambling funds or suspicious?

2. If such risks exist even after full tax compliance, should Indian users continue trusting CoinDCX, or should we simply delete the app to protect ourselves?

3. What is the meaning of a P2P exchange if, after tax deduction, withdrawals are still blocked by banks and flagged by authorities?

4. Is CoinDCX registered as a third party app with Indian banks, or why is there no direct coordination with banks to prevent such issues?

5. Why has my support ticket on this matter received no proper response so far?

—> If this problem is not addressed with a clear and transparent solution, then users will be forced to assume that CoinDCX’s P2P services are unsafe or misleading.

I request an urgent clarification from your team or leadership regarding this matter.

𝐔𝐩𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞: No resolution yet from X Corp. Support.

I have formally filed complaints with the Internet Crime Complaint Center (𝐈𝐂𝟑 – 𝐅𝐁𝐈 𝐜𝐲𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧) and the 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐚 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥’𝐬 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞

Acknowledgments attached below.

This involves unauthorized access, email change, and loss of a verified, monetized account with 16K+ followers — without any prior alert or recovery assistance.

Requesting immediate intervention from @Support @Safety.

#IC3 #CAAttorneyGeneral #AccountHacked #CyberSecurity

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

Tag your friends jo P2P karte hain!

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). text: #HearingUpdate Petitioner v NIXI & Ors. WP(C) No. 15332 of 2026 in respect of the suspension of https://t.co/VlAn1E1reI, (1/n) https://t.co/QKQQz3aGY3

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.
Can a democracy be judged by its election results if the voter list itself can’t be checked? https://t.co/nXYaDaiYXc
Since June 2025, the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) has left more than 130 million names off India’s draft voter rolls. https://t.co/LJsRNpmidf

It runs on software that nobody outside the Commission can inspect.
Based on Analysis by IFF Founder Director Apar Gupta's Analysis for @techpolicypress 
Read the whole analysis :https://t.co/y24EY4V6Be https://t.co/R7P5UCkTfA

I’ve written an essay for @techpolicypress on the SIR and the faith in digitisation that has shaped Indian elections. I wanted to understand how decisions about who can vote came to depend on software whose workings are closed to public scrutiny.

For the research, over some weekends in the IIC library, I read books by former Chief Election Commissioners. I enjoyed them, particularly the accounts of the logistical work involved in conducting elections at this scale. Technology, though, is almost always presented as a success. For instance, former CEC S.Y. Quraishi recalls facial recognition software in Manipur detecting a woman who had come to vote more than 60 times in different guises. H.S. Brahma began linking voter IDs with Aadhaar on the promise that almost every complaint about the rolls would be resolved. These accounts say much more about what technology promises than about its limits.That faith extends well beyond the Commission as across Indian public policy, digitisation is routinely offered as the answer to failures of administration (in panels called, "state capacity constraints"). 

However, when the rules, or more properly the updates in the software builds in a system are kept secret, or changed to vary from the officially notified forms, however, discretion becomes harder to examine. People affected by an arbitrary decision have fewer means of understanding or challenging it. I also went back to an earlier attempt to make voters prove their entitlement to remain on the rolls. In 1992, the Commission under T.N. Seshan instructed its officers that the burden of proving citizenship lay on the voter. An officer in Delhi then declared an entire slum colony of 18,000 residents suspected foreigners. More than 16,000 lost their vote. In Lal Babu Hussein in 1995, the Supreme Court held that an existing entry on the roll carried a presumption that the registering officer had followed the law. The intensive revision of 2002–04 proceeded on that basis. Enumerators did the verification, and existing voters were presumed to belong on the rolls.

The SIR reverses that presumption through a process dependent on software. Today, more than 130 million names have come off draft rolls. The software treated “Md” and “Mohammed” as different people, flagged siblings born less than nine months apart, including twins, and found seven siblings sharing a father suspicious. Its rules, error rates and audit results have not been published. Voters are left to correct these errors, often by standing in queues and responding to notices in languages they cannot read. Nandan Nilekani, whose book advocated a centralised voter database and digitisation, has himself received an SIR notice. Finally, I would like to thank Tech Policy Press and its patient editorial team for being kind and gentle with me. Please read the essay and let me know what you think of it.
